plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional surface plot enclosed in a thin rectangular wireframe box, with no axis labels, tick marks, or numerical scales shown. A broad flat blue sheet spans the box at mid-height, standing for the level far from the charges. On the right half of the sheet the surface rises into a steep, narrow peak whose flanks are banded in pink and violet and whose tip is cut off flat. On the left half the surface plunges into a matching funnel-shaped depression, shaded the same way and likewise truncated at its base. Dark contour lines run across the surface as closed loops encircling both the peak and the pit, crowding together where the surface steepens and spreading into wide rounded loops out on the flat sheet, with a faint straight line crossing the sheet between the two features. Rendering potential as height converts the sign and size of the potential into visible relief, so the hill and the trough can be read against each other directly. The plot builds intuition for the potential of two equal and opposite charges carried on conducting spheres of finite radius.

elements: thin transparent rectangular wireframe plotting box enclosing the whole surface
broad rectangular blue reference sheet at zero electric potential spanning most of the box
continuous electric-potential surface coincident with the blue sheet far from the charges
right-hand positive-potential hill rising above the sheet, steep and narrow near the charge
flat truncated circular cap at the top of the right-hand positive hill representing finite conducting-sphere radius
left-hand negative-potential well descending below the sheet, steep and narrow near the charge
flat truncated circular cap at the bottom of the left-hand negative well representing finite conducting-sphere radius
pink-to-violet height bands on the positive hill and negative well
dark contour lines drawn on the potential surface
closed crowded contour loops around the positive hill
closed crowded contour loops around the negative well
wide rounded contour loops spreading across the flatter blue sheet between and around the charges
faint straight diagonal contour/zero-crossing line running across the sheet between the two features
two invisible source centers used to compute the potential: negative source on the left half and positive source on the right half

interactions.label: Charge balance
interactions.teaches: Changing the relative positive and negative source strengths changes the hill and well heights, so the sign of potential and the relative magnitude of each charge can be read directly from the surface relief

interactions.label: Representation
interactions.teaches: The same potential field can be read either as height or as level curves; crowded contours mark the steep parts of the surface where the potential changes fastest

interactions.label: Charge separation
interactions.teaches: Moving the opposite charges together or apart shifts the hill, trough, and contour loops, revealing how the total potential is the superposition of the two source potentials

demo_steps.title: Equal and opposite charges
demo_steps.narration: The default view shows a positive hill on the right and a matching negative well on the left. Their similar height and depth indicate equal magnitude with opposite sign.

demo_steps.title: Unequal source strengths
demo_steps.narration: Shift the balance toward the positive charge. The right-hand hill becomes taller than the left-hand well is deep, and the surrounding contour pattern is pulled toward the stronger source.

demo_steps.title: Contour reading
demo_steps.narration: Flattening to the contour view keeps the same level curves. The loops remain most crowded near each charge, showing that the potential gradient is largest where the surface was steepest.

demo_steps.title: Change the separation
demo_steps.narration: Bring the charges closer together. The hill and trough approach each other, and the contours between them squeeze and reshape because the two potentials overlap more strongly.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use an axonometric/isometric-like view matching the source: the rectangular plot plane is seen from above, with screen-right corresponding roughly to +X and the receding diagonal corresponding to +Z; electric potential height is +Y. Plot box approximately X=7.0 units wide, Z=5.0 units deep, Y from -2.0 to +2.0. Zero-potential sheet lies at Y=0 and fills about X=[-3.4,3.4], Z=[-2.4,2.4]. Wireframe box is a transparent rectangular prism enclosing the sheet and relief; use thin black or dark gray lines #222222 with no shaded faces. Negative source is on the left/front-left half of the sheet, default center approximately X=-1.7, Z=-0.35; positive source is on the right/back-right half, default center approximately X=+1.7, Z=+0.35. The separation slider should move these centers symmetrically along this left-front to right-back diagonal, not purely horizontally: negative at (-d/2, -0.10d) and positive at (+d/2, +0.10d) is a good match. Compute potential as V(x,z)=Apos/sqrt((x-xpos)^2+(z-zpos)^2+a^2) - Aneg/sqrt((x-xneg)^2+(z-zneg)^2+a^2), with finite-radius cutoff a about 0.28 to 0.35 units so the hill and well have flat truncated caps rather than singular spikes. For chargeBalance b, use Apos=1+b and Aneg=1-b, clamped to a small positive minimum such as 0.05; default b=0 gives equal and opposite charges. Scale height so default peak and trough reach about ±1.45 world units, leaving margin inside the wireframe box. Color palette: zero sheet and far surface light blue #8ec9ee to #9bd3f3; contour lines dark navy/black #111827; peak/well banding should transition through pale cyan #9bd3f3, lavender #b8a6ff, violet #8150d6, pink #f4a0b8, and peach #ffd0a8 near the truncated extreme. Positive hill is on the right and rises upward; negative well is on the left and descends below the blue sheet. In contour-only mode the height should smoothly flatten to Y=0 while retaining the same contour loops in plan view.
interactionPlan.notes: Generate the surface as a dense grid mesh, at least 120 by 90 samples, with vertex colors based on signed potential and height bands. Draw contours using marching squares on the same sampled potential values, then project contour polylines onto the current surface for surface mode and onto Y=0 for contour mode. Use a small polygon offset or slight Y offset to prevent z-fighting between contours and the surface. The truncated caps can be implemented by clamping |V| before height scaling and shading the top/bottom cap as nearly flat. Animate transitions for the viewMode toggle so the learner sees the surface collapse into the contour map rather than abruptly switching.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for charge balance: vary the positive and negative source strengths and the surface peak/well heights update, showing electric potential sign and relative magnitude.
- Toggle between surface and contour views: the learner switches representations, the raised/lowered surface flattens into contour loops with the same crowded spacing near charges, showing that steep height changes correspond to strong potential gradients.
- Slider for charge separation: the learner moves the equal and opposite charges apart or together, the hill, trough, and contour loops shift accordingly, clarifying how superposed potentials shape the region between conducting spheres.

authoredContext:
To improve your intuition, we show a three-dimensional variant of the potential in a system with two opposing charges. The figure displays a three-dimensional map of electric potential, where lines on the map are for equipotential surfaces. The hill is at the positive charge, and the trough is at the negative charge. The potential is zero far away from the charges. Note that the cut off at a particular potential implies that the charges are on conducting spheres with a finite radius.

Electric potential map of two opposite charges of equal magnitude on conducting spheres. The potential is negative near the negative charge and positive near the positive charge.

The illustration shows electric potential map and equipotential lines two charges – one positive and one negative.

A two-dimensional map of the cross-sectional plane that contains both charges is shown in the figure. The line that is equidistant from the two opposite charges corresponds to zero potential, since at the points on the line, the positive potential from the positive charge cancels the negative potential from the negative charge. Equipotential lines in the cross-sectional plane are closed loops, which are not necessarily circles, since at each point, the net potential is the sum of the potentials from each charge.

discrepancies: The generated surface is a continuous dark, semi-transparent height field over the whole blue sheet, whereas the source reads more like a lighter blue base plane with localized colored hill/well features and contour curves.
The negative well is visually muted and partly obscured compared with the source, where the depression has stronger concentric colored bands and a clearer deep center.
The generated figure includes a faint straight diagonal zero-guide line that is not apparent in the source figure.
The contour pattern differs in placement and density, especially between the two charges, where the source has more open sweeping curves and less uniformly distributed contouring.
The initial camera/view places the positive hill more toward the front-right than the source's upper-right composition, slightly changing the spatial resemblance.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is clearly recognizable as the same electric-potential surface with a hill, well, contours, plane, and box, but the surface opacity, contour layout, and extra guide line reduce visual fidelity.
action_items: Lighten the blue base plane and reduce the dark overlay effect so it more closely matches the pale cyan sheet in the source.
Make the negative well deeper and more visually distinct with stronger colored contour bands near its center.
Remove or hide the faint diagonal zero-guide line unless it is explicitly part of the source figure.
Adjust the initial camera orientation and charge placement so the positive hill appears closer to the upper-right layout of the reference.
